newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia's property prices seen rising in long term.
newsitem.headline: Asia's property prices seen rising in long term.

text.p: Asia's property prices are expected to rise in the long-term, but the immediate outlook is mixed, a regional consultancy said.
The Political and Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd said in its latest survey Hong Kong's property prices had potential for a rise when the British colony returned to Chinese rule in mid-1997.

The Hong Kong-based consultancy said prices could get a boost as companies realised that the political transition would not eliminate Hong Kong's attraction as a regional business centre, and as China stepped up its investments in the territory.
But it said Hong Kong's property market was likely to remain relatively stable between now and next July. Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997.

The firm cited a survey conducted in October by the Swiss Business Council in Hong Kong which said uncertainties surrounding the territory's transition would quickly dissipate after next July, and Hong Kong's dynamism would be back to normal by 1998.

However, the consultancy's report said if prices between now and next July remained high, investors would review which operations they kept in Hong Kong and which could be moved to more cost-effective locations.

In Jakarta and Malaysia, downward pressure on office rentals was likely next year. Jakarta was expected to digest additional supply of 292,000 square metres (314,000 square feet) of office space and Malaysia an estimated seven million square feet (6.5 million square metres), the report said.

Property consultants estimated that 1997 could see rentals fall by 5 percent in Malaysia' prime areas, while secondary locations in the capital, Kuala Lumpur, could decline as much as 10 percent, the report said.

In the Philippines however, the real estate sector was booming, buoyed by the country's strong economic growth and relative political stability. Real estate industry insiders expected rents to rise by 10 percent to 15 percent over the next three years, but they said rents were still competitive compared to other Asian cities, the report said.

Singapore's focus had swung from rising prices and high rentals last year and early this year, to talk of market consolidation and forced selling next year, as speculators found themselves unable to service loans, the report said.

In the longer term, however, property prices in the high economic growth region were expected to rise. The report said while an oversupply problem appeared inevitable in 1997, the vacant spaces would soon be filled up to spur a price rise.

"A company might be able to negotiate a very favourable price for its factory site, but once it moves in and gears up operation, it will usually discover quickly that a severe shortage of suitable housing for its expatriate staff pushes up prices for what little space is available, to extremely high levels," it said.
"The pace of property development is too slow to satisfy the high growth in demand from international companies investing in the region," the report said.
